sections.body_md:
A lower bound is not the same thing as a point where the bound is achieved. Existence is the question of whether the argmin set is nonempty. Two sufficient situations cover most of the smooth problems in this subject.

The first is compactness. In real space a set is compact when it is closed and bounded. A continuous function on a nonempty compact set attains its minimum and its maximum. The closed unit disk is compact. An open disk is not, and a line is not. The theorem does not say the minimizer is interior. On a disk it often sits on the boundary.

The second situation is an unbounded set, where compactness is unavailable. A continuous function that is coercive, meaning the values tend to infinity as the norm does, still attains a minimum on a nonempty closed set. Coercivity makes the sublevel sets bounded, continuity makes them closed, and a feasible point makes one of them nonempty. Coercivity is sufficient and not necessary. A sine attains its minimum on the line without tending to infinity.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md: If \(\mathcal{X}\) is nonempty and compact and \(f\) is continuous, there exists \(x^\star \in \mathcal{X}\) with \(f(x^\star) = \inf_{\mathcal{X}} f\). If \(\mathcal{X}\) is nonempty and closed, \(f\) is continuous, and \(f(x) \to +\infty\) as \(\lVert x \rVert \to \infty\) with \(x \in \mathcal{X}\), the same conclusion holds. A sublevel set \(\{x \in \mathcal{X}: f(x) \le f(x_0)\}\) of a coercive continuous function is compact once it is nonempty.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Minimize \((x - 2)^2 + (y + 1)^2 + 11\) over the closed disk of radius 5 centered at the origin. The squares vanish at \((2, -1)\). That point has norm \(\sqrt{5}\), which is less than 5, so it is feasible. The disk minimum is 11, and it is attained at that single interior point.

The same function on the whole plane has the same minimizer, now by coercivity rather than by compactness: the squares dominate at infinity. If the added constant were removed, the minimum value would change and the minimizer would not. If the disk were replaced by its interior, this particular minimizer would remain feasible. A minimizer on the boundary would not survive that opening.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Closed is not enough, and bounded is not enough. The half-line of nonnegative reals is closed and unbounded, and \(e^{-t}\) decreases toward 0 without attaining it. The open interval \((0, 1)\) is bounded and not closed, and the identity has infimum 0 with no minimizer. Applying the compact-set theorem to either set is the usual false step. A stationary point is also not an existence proof. The exponential on the line has no stationary point and no minimizer. A coercive function can have both.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Once a minimizer is known to exist, the next work is to name it. For a smooth unconstrained problem the candidates are the stationary points, and the second-order test classifies them. Coercivity of a positive definite quadratic is the reason that quadratic has a minimizer before anyone solves the linear system.
